steps.intro: An adjective can describe a noun (“the great king”) or say something about it (“the king is great”). Listen for the difference: it's in the word “the”.

cards.title: Adjectives match their noun
body: An adjective takes the same endings as nouns, matching its noun's gender and number: טוֹב, good, is טוֹבָה with a feminine noun, טוֹבִים and טוֹבוֹת with plurals.

cards.title: “The great king”: after the noun, with “the”
body: To describe a noun, the adjective comes after it and copies its “the”: הַמֶּלֶךְ הַגָּדוֹל, “the king the great”, means the great king. Without “the” on either, אִישׁ צַדִּיק is “a righteous man”.
Grammar books call this the attributive use.

examples.en: the great city: feminine, like עִיר

cards.title: “The king is great”: no “the”, and no “is”
body: To say something about a noun, the adjective has no “the”, and often comes first: טוֹב הַדָּבָר, “good the word”, means the word is good.
Hebrew doesn't need a word for “is” or “am” here. Two nouns side by side make a sentence too: אֲנִי יְהוָה, “I the LORD”, means “I am the LORD”.
Grammar books call these the predicate use and the verbless (nominal) sentence.

cards.explain: The adjective comes after the noun and has “the” too, so it describes it: the great king.
The adjective has no “the” and comes first, so it says something about the noun: the word is good.

cards.prompt: Match each adjective to its meaning.

cards.explain: It matches עִיר (feminine, one) and copies its “the”: the great city.
Two nouns side by side make a sentence; Hebrew needs no word for “am”.

cards.prompt: Write “the great king”, starting on the right.
cards.explain: Noun first, then the adjective, both with “the”: הַמֶּלֶךְ הַגָּדוֹל.

steps.intro: Find each adjective: does it describe its noun, or say something about it?

cards.note: קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת: the adjective first, with no “is”: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts.”
כִּי טוֹב יְהֹוָה: “for the LORD is good”. טוֹב comes first, with no “the”.
